findings.paper_title: Appendix - Councils Medium Term Financial Plan 2026-2030
findings.headline: Council recently repaid all external loans (March 2026) but MRP costs rising by £200k in 2026/27, indicating shift from debt repayment to capital financing.
findings.detail: The council paid off its entire external loan portfolio in March 2026 (previously £3m of borrowing). However, MRP (the annual revenue charge for capital repayment) is rising by £200k in 2026/27 to £2m, and forecast to remain at £2m p.a. thereafter, reflecting the shift from historical debt repayment to revenue financing of new capital investment.
findings.matters: While debt repayment is positive, the rising MRP charges indicate the council's capital programme is shifting from borrowed funds to revenue-funded repayment. This increases pressure on revenue budgets and reduces flexibility.
findings.figures: External borrowing: £3m (31.12.25) → £0m (10.3.26); MRP budget 2026/27: £2m (up £200k from prior year)
findings.quote: The Council recently (10th March 2026) paid off all existing external loans and prior to the end of the 2025/26 financial year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix - Councils Medium Term Financial Plan 2026-2030
findings.headline: Budget forecasts built on significant uncertainties: central government funding levels unknown at time of planning, and global inflation/interest rate volatility elevated.
findings.detail: The council developed its 2026/27 Estimates "without absolute certainty of the amount of Rates Support Grant and other central government funding of direct service grants receivable in 2026/27." The Treasury Management Strategy cites heightened geopolitical risk (Iran conflict), material shift in interest rate outlook, and increased volatility in financial markets. These create planning risk around key assumptions.
findings.matters: Revenue and capital plans built on uncertain central government funding and volatile macroeconomic conditions are prone to mid-year reforecasting. A lender needs to know the council's buffer against assumption changes.
findings.figures: Budget assumptions include 3.5% annual staff cost increase, 2% recycling cost increase p.a., interest rates assumed at 3.8% average
findings.quote: The Estimates were developed without absolute certainty of the amount of Rates Support Grant and other central government funding of direct service grants receivable in 2026/27. The Department for Communities (DfC) and other central government Departments do not know their budgets for allocations to Councils until after the prescribed date of 15 February 2026.

findings.paper_title: Appendix - Councils Medium Term Financial Plan 2026-2030
findings.headline: Capital programme is subject to completion of business cases still under development, creating implementation and timing risk.
findings.detail: The MTFP states that "the estimated Capital Programme for 2026-2030 is still subject to a number of Council decisions on business cases, to be developed/currently under development, and may impact the outcome of the Capital Plan." The programme depends on external funding confirmation, completion of corporate strategies, and detailed design approval.
findings.matters: Incomplete business case assessment means capital plans may slip, be rescoped, or fail. For a lender, this creates uncertainty about the timing and scale of capital spend and therefore the trajectory of borrowing need.
findings.figures: Programme value £53.2m gross (£33m net of grant), consisting of committed and uncommitted projects
findings.quote: The Plan for 2026-30 is supported, in the majority, by approved business cases. However the estimated Capital Programme for 2026-2030 is still subject to a number of Council decisions on business cases, to be developed/currently under development, and may impact the outcome of the Capital Plan.

findings.paper_title: Appendix - Councils Medium Term Financial Plan 2026-2030
findings.headline: Rate increases will be needed to support capital investment, with council explicitly preferring managed rather than large single-year uplifts.
findings.detail: The MTFP acknowledges that rates increases will be required but states there is "a strong preference that rates increases required to support capital investment plans are considered in a managed way – i.e.: that there is not a large uplift in rates in one year as a result of investment in a project." This preference suggests concern about unmanaged rate volatility and affordability for residents.
findings.matters: Rate-setting decisions are highly political and a council's explicit concern about managing uplifts signals either that increases are imminent or that resistance is expected. This affects debt capacity and service sustainability.
findings.figures: Financing costs rising from 2.4% of net revenue stream (2025/26) to 2.7% (2026/27 onwards)
findings.quote: there is a strong preference that rates increases required to support capital investment plans are considered in a managed way – i.e.: that there is not a large uplift in rates in one year as a result of investment in a project

findings.paper_title: Appendix - Councils Medium Term Financial Plan 2026-2030
findings.headline: Treasury investments forecast to fall from £44m to £30.6m by 2030 as reserves are used to fund capital and revenue commitments.
findings.detail: The council currently holds £44m in treasury investments (as of 31 December 2025). The forecast shows this declining to £30.6m by 2030 as capital receipts are used for capital expenditure and reserves are drawn down for revenue support. The capital strategy notes the council will transition from net borrower (historically) to net investor, but with declining investment position.
findings.matters: A sustained decline in liquid reserves reduces financial flexibility and increases vulnerability to unexpected pressures. For a lender, this signals tightening cash headroom.
findings.figures: Treasury investments: £48m (31.3.25) → £42m (31.3.26 forecast) → £30.6m (31.3.30 forecast)
findings.quote: the liability benchmark shows that the level of investment is forecasted to reduce significantly

findings.paper_title: Appendix - Councils Medium Term Financial Plan 2026-2030
findings.headline: Capital programme of £26.4m requires substantial reserve drawdown and future rate increases, with long-term affordability still under analysis.
findings.detail: The council's four-year capital programme requires £26.4m of council-funded expenditure. This will be funded primarily through existing reserves and future rates, as the council plans not to borrow in 2026/27. The MTFP explicitly states that "long term affordability and the impact of funding raised through rates requires further analysis" and that "further financial planning is required to balance the cost-of-service delivery with the ambitious Capital Plans."
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can afford its capital plans without unsustainable rate increases or reserve depletion. The fact that detailed affordability analysis is still pending is a risk factor.
findings.figures: £26.4m council-funded capital; £18.6m external funding assumed (total programme £45m); capital programme described as "significantly lower in value than previously programmes"
findings.quote: Overall, the level of investment proposed by the Council (excluding any grant or other external funding) of £26.4m over the next four years 2026-2030, will require substantial financial support which can only be funded through the use of existing reserves, directly on the current and future rates and to meet loan commitments.

findings.paper_title: Robustness of the Estimates and Adequacy of Reserves for the Financial Year 202627
findings.headline: Investment income of £400k included in rates base, but officers note this is dependent on declining interest rates and depleting cash reserves
findings.detail: Council has benefited from c.£1.9m annually from investment income since late 2022, not previously budgeted for. For 2026/27, officers including £400k as a 'saving' in the rates base. However, officers explicitly note dependency: 'the interest the Council receives from its investments are subject to change and dependant on a number of factors including; there being cash available to invest, the amount of cash available, the interest rates (which are decreasing)'. This creates a recurring revenue line dependent on volatile market rates and declining asset base.
findings.matters: Recurring revenue estimate heavily dependent on volatile market interest rates and declining cash reserves as the council depletes reserves by £600k annually; reversal risk as rates continue to fall.
findings.figures: £1.9m annual investment income since 2023/24; proposing £400k for 2026/27
findings.quote: Members to note that the interest the Council receives from its investments are subject to change and dependant on a number of factors including; there being cash available to invest, the amount of cash available, the interest rates (which are decreasing)

findings.paper_title: Robustness of the Estimates and Adequacy of Reserves for the Financial Year 202627
findings.headline: Residual waste contract savings delayed indefinitely by legal challenge; officers not including expected savings in 2026/27 estimates
findings.detail: Ongoing legal challenge to the award of contract for haulage, treatment and disposal of residual municipal waste in two lots. Officers note 'due to process and court timeframes, it is unlikely that the Council will be in a position to award these contracts in this financial year'. As a result, 'officers are not currently proposing to reflect any of the potential savings from the award of those contracts as part of rates estimates 26/27'. This defers an expected income/saving item.
findings.matters: Expected cost savings deferred indefinitely due to legal challenge; creates budget uncertainty and signals procurement risk in the council's service delivery model.
findings.figures: Quantum of expected savings not quantified in document
findings.quote: Due to process and court timeframes, it is unlikely that the Council will be in a position to award these contracts in this financial year. Therefore, officers are not currently proposing to reflect any of the potential savings from the award of those contracts as part of rates estimates 26/27

findings.paper_title: Robustness of the Estimates and Adequacy of Reserves for the Financial Year 202627
findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility income jumped £1.518m above estimate (provisional £3.371m to actual £4.889m), yet officers budget only 18% of payment into recurring rates
findings.detail: 2025/26 provisional estimate was £3.371m; actual payment was £4.889m. For 2026/27, officers proposing only £100k additional (approximately 18% of overall EPR payment). Officers take prudent approach, noting 'it would not be prudent to put the full allocation' into rates base and citing risk that 'in the event there is a shortfall in recovery of funds from producers, this may result in recalculations for local authorities and reduction in funding'. Officers await final clarity on expenditure conditions; any surplus goes to reserves for environmental projects.
findings.matters: Material income source with high volatility and uncertain conditions; the decision to exclude 82% of the payment from recurring revenue base suggests officers do not consider this funding sustainable or certain.
findings.figures: 2025/26 provisional £3.371m, actual £4.889m (increase £1.518m, +45%); 2026/27 proposing additional £100k; officers include approximately 18% of overall payment
findings.quote: Officers remain of the view that it would not be prudent to put the full allocation as notified to this Council towards its rates estimate. Officers have been advised that in the event there is a shortfall in recovery of funds from producers, this may result in recalculations for local authorities and reduction in funding

findings.paper_title: Robustness of the Estimates and Adequacy of Reserves for the Financial Year 202627
findings.headline: Rate support grant allocation revised downward 14 January with uncertainty unresolved; Estimated Penny Product recalculated 30 January after minister stopped revaluation 29 January
findings.detail: RSG allocation cut from 15.92% to 13.29% on 14 January, then partially restored with most recent position (2 February) indicating reduction but 'not as low as 13.29%'. Separately, EPP was being recalculated from November, then revised 30 January after minister stopped Reval 2026 without notice on 29 January. Officers 'moderated' the revised EPP upward based on prudent assessment of debt write-off risk. These critical income assumptions were revised days before rates were struck. Prior year showed £493,755 clawback due to LPS error in non-domestic valuation.
findings.matters: Critical income assumptions undergo material revision in the days before rates are set, creating volatility in the revenue base and justifying the council's reserve depletion strategy as a response to structural income uncertainty.
findings.figures: RSG: 15.92% (2025/26) cut to 13.29% (14 Jan 2026), then partially restored (by 2 Feb); prior year clawback £493,755 due to NAV error; domestic growth c.0.38%
findings.quote: However, late on 29th January 2026 and without notice, correspondence was received from the Minister of Finance that he had instructed LPS to stop the implementation process of Reval 2026

findings.paper_title: Robustness of the Estimates and Adequacy of Reserves for the Financial Year 202627
findings.headline: Council approaching capital borrowing: officers signal debt-funded capital investment likely within next electoral term
findings.detail: Officers state explicitly it is 'now possible that the Council will commence funding its capital expenditure by borrowing within the next term of the Council'. Timing depends on RSG allocation, revenue pressures, and capital ambitions. Current capital spend £6.6m planned for 2025/26 with £26m total over 2026-2030. Council has funded capital from cash reserves to date but these are declining as the reserve depletion strategy continues. Capital Financing Requirement is £10.4m.
findings.matters: Signals the council's financial flexibility is spent and capital investment will now carry debt service costs, reducing the revenue budget available for service delivery.
findings.figures: Net capital spend 2024/25 £5.5m; 2025/26 £6.6m estimated; 2026-2030 total £26m; Capital Financing Requirement £10.4m at 31 March 2025; current recurrent capital funding reduced to £1.1m from £1.5m (2023/24); Mid-South West Growth Deal reduced to £700k from £1m (2023/24)
findings.quote: it is now possible that the Council will commence funding its capital expenditure by borrowing within the next term of the Council

findings.paper_title: Robustness of the Estimates and Adequacy of Reserves for the Financial Year 202627
findings.headline: Council committing to systematic reserve depletion strategy: £6m drawn down over four years (2023/24 to 2026/27) to suppress district rate increases
findings.detail: Starting with £2.4m in 2023/24, the council has drawn £1.8m (2024/25) and £1.2m (2025/26), with £0.6m proposed for 2026/27. Officers warn this depletion strategy creates risk: with further £600k pressure appearing in 2027/28 after the £6m exhausts, they caution that exceeding this envelope 'could significantly increase the risk of the Council's reserves becoming inadequate'. The strategy masks structural revenue pressures rather than resolving them.
findings.matters: Planned reserve depletion to manage rates politically rather than structurally signals the council's inability to fund recurrent expenditure from recurring income, and commits the council to either service cuts or new borrowing once reserves exhaust.
findings.quote: further application of cash balances in excess of the £6m (which was the consequence of applying a £2.4m balance in 2023/24) could significantly increase the risk of the Council's reserves becoming inadequate

findings.paper_title: Appendix - Performance Improvement Local Government Auditor’s Audit and Assessment (Section 95) Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Performance improvement function managed by a single officer with no backup, continuing a prior-year business continuity risk.
findings.detail: The council's entire performance improvement function is managed by one Corporate Performance and Quality Officer (CPQO). A proposal for improvement was made in the 2024-25 audit regarding the isolated nature of this role and lack of business continuity arrangements. No additional staff have been added to the team in the intervening year. The CPQO has prepared a 'How to Guide' document to mitigate this risk, but the structural dependency remains.
findings.matters: Single-person dependency creates operational risk; illness, departure, or absence of this officer could disrupt performance monitoring and statutory compliance; the risk persists despite being flagged in the prior year.
findings.figures: One person in performance improvement team; no new staff added in current year
findings.quote: A proposal for improvement was made in the 2024-25 S95 report in relation to the isolated nature of the CPQO and lack of business continuity arrangements in place. At present there are no new members of staff in the performance improvement team.

findings.paper_title: Appendix - Performance Improvement Local Government Auditor’s Audit and Assessment (Section 95) Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Economic development statistics for business approvals contain unverified errors affecting approximately 7.5% of reported figures.
findings.detail: An internal audit review by Belfast City Council (which collates economic development figures for all Northern Ireland councils) identified that 189 business plan approvals—approximately 7.5 percent of the year's total—have unreliable figures. These figures feed into the Department for the Economy's statutory indicator reporting. Mid Ulster flagged this in their Self-Assessment Report, but the figures remain unverified and BCC is undertaking further work to assess inclusion.
findings.matters: Data integrity issues in one performance area suggest potential systematic weaknesses in data collection or validation processes; if reported figures contain errors, this raises confidence issues for stakeholders reviewing council performance.
findings.figures: 189 business plan approvals out of approximately 2,500 total (7.5%)
findings.quote: The Internal Audit review identified that the figures relating to 189 business plan approvals (approximately 7.5 per cent of the total approvals for the year) are not reliable.

findings.paper_title: Appendix - Performance Improvement Local Government Auditor’s Audit and Assessment (Section 95) Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Performance improvement data lacks internal audit validation and independent verification of accuracy.
findings.detail: Internal Audit does not review the performance improvement function or validate figures in the Self-Assessment Report. Only the external auditor (NIAO) reviews compliance with legislative requirements, but does not validate the accuracy of data reported. The auditors have made a formal proposal for improvement that Internal Audit should audit the performance improvement function to provide assurance over data integrity.
findings.matters: Without internal audit validation, there is reduced assurance over the accuracy of performance figures the council reports publicly and to government; weaknesses in data integrity processes could affect other financial or operational reporting.
findings.figures: One Corporate Performance and Quality Officer responsible for all performance improvement data collection and reporting, with no independent internal audit validation
findings.quote: Internal Audit do not carry out any work on the Performance Improvement function there is therefore no data validation on figures within the Self-Assessment Report (SAR).

findings.paper_title: Appendix - Performance Improvement Local Government Auditor’s Audit and Assessment (Section 95) Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Planning service has missed statutory targets for two consecutive years with all three indicators declining.
findings.detail: Mid Ulster failed to meet statutory indicators for planning in 2024-25, continuing a pattern from the prior year. All three planning performance indicators show downward trends: average processing times for major planning applications, average processing times for local planning applications, and the percentage of enforcement cases processed within 39 weeks. The auditor specifically noted this as concerning and proposed an in-depth analysis of the planning system.
findings.matters: Planning service underperformance can reduce the council's ability to collect planning fees, delay economic development, and indicate resource constraints or management issues affecting broader service delivery.
findings.figures: All three planning indicators declining; specific targets for major and local planning processing times not met in 2024-25 (and 2023-24)
findings.quote: The Council has not met statutory planning indicators for the second year in a row. In the 2024-25 period all three indicators have demonstrated a downward trend.

findings.paper_title: Appendix - Review of Treasury Management Policy
findings.headline: Document is in draft with unresolved uncertainties and outdated information
findings.detail: The policy contains multiple tracked changes, editorial comments, and internal queries (e.g., 'What is it currently? Our Capital Plan is agreed but could be amended throughout the year so this needs tweaked a little'). It also mixes dates from different years (2017/18, 2023/24) and contains contradictory interest rate guidance (references to a 0.25% base rate alongside a September 2023 5.25% forecast), suggesting the document has not been properly updated or signed off.
findings.matters: A policy document this incomplete suggests either inadequate governance processes or that the council is still working through treasury management strategy decisions; neither instils confidence that treasury risk is being actively managed.
findings.figures: None; document control shows multiple unresolved comments and version inconsistencies
findings.quote: Commented [CM14]: What is it currently? Our Capital Plan is agreed but could be amended throughout the year so this needs tweaked a little.

findings.paper_title: Appendix - Review of Treasury Management Policy
findings.headline: Council holds approximately £35m in invested cash balances while planning to be a long-term net borrower
findings.detail: The council maintains significant treasury investment balances (approximately £35m over the past 6 months, expected to continue), which are invested in short-term, low-risk instruments for liquidity management. This occurs while the council anticipates being a long-term net borrower, creating an apparent mismatch between cash holdings and borrowing strategy.
findings.matters: The strategy of holding large cash reserves while simultaneously borrowing suggests either earmarked reserves for specific purposes or suboptimal cash management; a lender needs to understand whether these balances are genuinely available to reduce debt or are committed elsewhere.
findings.figures: Approximately £35 million treasury investment balance
findings.quote: In the past 6 months, the Authority'sCouncil's treasury investment balance has been approximately £35 million, and similar levels are expected to be maintained in the forthcoming year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix - Review of Treasury Management Policy
findings.headline: Capital borrowing requirement of £14.5m for the financial year, subject to change as capital programme is finalised
findings.detail: The council's net capital borrowing requirement is estimated at £14.5m but carries explicit uncertainty: the figure could change when the capital programme is agreed or amended during the year. Borrowing will come from the Northern Ireland Consolidated Fund or the commercial market. The timing of drawdown directly impacts interest costs.
findings.matters: The capital borrowing plan is both material and uncertain; a lender needs to know the actual size and timing of new debt obligations to assess debt trajectory and capacity.
findings.figures: £14.5m net capital borrowing requirement
findings.quote: The Council's net capital borrowing requirement for 202317/1824 is presently estimated at £14.5m, but this could vary when the draftif the capital programme is agreed or if it is amended during the year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix - Review of Treasury Management Policy
findings.headline: Existing debt is locked into unfavorable terms due to refinancing penalties
findings.detail: The council has existing loans where early redemption penalties outweigh the benefit of refinancing at lower rates. Officers note this situation is unlikely to change and that restructuring would only become cost-effective if the Northern Ireland Assembly subsidises the financial penalties imposed by the Northern Ireland Consolidated Fund. This leaves the council unable to reduce borrowing costs if rates fall.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council cannot easily adjust its debt profile if financial conditions change; the council is structurally committed to high-cost debt, which affects its financial flexibility and future creditworthiness.
findings.figures: Existing loans with redemption penalties; no quantum given
findings.quote: Recent instigations have concluded that penalties in respect of early redemption of loans outweigh the benefits of re-financing the loans at lower interest rates. The officers believe that this is unlikely to change and that restructuring will only be cost effective if the Northern Ireland Assembly is prepared to underwrite/subsidise the financial penalties which will be levied by the NICF.
